      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The adaptation of Hitchens's maxim asserts nearly universal religious harm without supplying reasons for that breadth. The surrounding progress examples do not establish it. This is a joking aside, followed by explicit credit to Christianity's understanding of human nature (E1655–E1672), which qualifies its seriousness; no device immunizes it against objections."
    },

      "quote": "we don't know the world can be different",
      "form": "no",

        "none"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Responding to the proposed heaven without earthly suffering (E1947–E1953), McGrath requires a comparison world before accepting that things could differ. This may shield theism by setting an unavailable comparison requirement, but could be a limited objection about possibility. He earlier acknowledges suffering as a legitimate difficulty (E1817–E1825); this is an argument, not a slogan."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2078,
      "endEvent": 2085,
      "contextStartEvent": 2056,
      "contextEndEvent": 2152,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "God sacrificed himself to himself to save us from himself",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "ridicule"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The formula compresses Shermer's objection that God could forgive without incarnation and suffering (E2071–E2077), so it has an argumentative basis. Calling the account 'barking mad' may additionally substitute apparent absurdity for demonstrating incoherence. McGrath supplies a meaning-centered interpretation afterward (E2102–E2152); Shermer does not declare all possible replies inadmissible."
    }
